title: Memory, GC & Span<T>
summary: Stack versus heap in practice, the generational GC and the large object heap, what allocates (strings, boxing, closures, LINQ), Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> for allocation-free slicing, and ArrayPool.
lesson:
## Where values live (the useful approximation)

- **Locals of value types** (an `int`, a small struct) live in the method's stack frame or inside whatever contains them.
- **Objects** (class instances, arrays, strings, boxed values, closures) are allocated on the **managed heap** and cleaned up by the garbage collector.

The real rule is "value types live where their container lives": an `int` field of a class is on the heap, inside that object.

## The generational GC

New objects start in **generation 0**. A gen-0 collection is fast and frequent; objects that survive move to gen 1, then gen 2. `GC.MaxGeneration` is 2. Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go straight to the **large object heap** (collected with gen 2), so allocating big temporary arrays repeatedly is expensive.

Most objects die young, which is why short-lived allocations are cheap but not free: every allocation brings the next collection closer, and in a busy API, allocations per request translate directly into GC pauses and CPU.

## What allocates, often unnoticed

- **Strings**: every `Substring`, `Split`, `+`, `ToLower`, `string.Format` creates new strings.
- **Boxing**: putting a value type into `object` or a non-generic interface (`ArrayList`, `string.Format("{0}", 42)` in old APIs, `IComparable` on a struct).
- **Closures**: a lambda that captures locals allocates a closure object (and a delegate).
- **LINQ**: iterators and delegates per call; fine in normal code, avoidable in hot loops.
- **params arrays**, `ToList()` copies, async state machines for methods that actually await.

Measure before optimising: `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()`, BenchmarkDotNet with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, or `dotnet-counters`.

## Span<T>: a view, not a copy

`Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` represent a contiguous slice of memory (an array, a string, stack memory) without copying it:

```csharp
ReadOnlySpan<char> s = "2026-11-04".AsSpan();
int year  = int.Parse(s[..4]);        // no Substring, no new string
int month = int.Parse(s.Slice(5, 2));

var arr = new[] { 10, 20, 30 };
Span<int> tail = arr.AsSpan(1);
tail[0] = 99;                         // writes through: arr is now [10, 99, 30]

Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[256];   // stack memory, no heap allocation
```

Spans are **ref structs**: they can live only on the stack, so they cannot be fields of classes, be captured by lambdas, or live across `await`. For those cases use `Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>`, which can be stored and sliced the same way.

Most parsing APIs (`int.Parse`, `DateOnly.TryParse`, `Utf8JsonReader`, `string.Split` successors) accept spans.

## Reusing buffers

`ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(size)` hands out an array of AT LEAST that size from a pool; `Return` it when done (and never use it afterwards). It avoids allocating a new large buffer per request for things like stream copies and compression. Buckets are powers of two, so `Rent(1000)` returns a 1,024-element array: keep the length you asked for next to it. Returned arrays are not cleared by default, so pass `clearArray: true` to `Return` when the buffer held tokens or personal data.

## When to care

For typical CRUD endpoints, database round-trips dominate and allocation tuning is irrelevant. It matters in hot paths: parsing large files, serialisation, middleware that runs on every request, and high-throughput services. Clarity first; Span where a profiler says so. One 20 ms database round-trip costs more than many thousands of small allocations, so a request that makes 40 queries gains nothing from removing a `Substring`. Fix the queries, measure again, and reach for spans and pooling only where the numbers still point at allocation.

quiz.prompt: In which generation does a newly allocated small object start?
choices: Gen 2
The large object heap
Gen 0
Gen 1
quiz.explanation: The allocator hands out small objects from the gen-0 budget, filling it by bumping a pointer, so every new small object is gen 0. A gen-0 collection examines only those young objects; the ones still referenced are promoted to gen 1 and, if they survive again, to gen 2. Gen 2 holds long-lived survivors and is never where a new small object starts, and only objects of 85,000 bytes or more skip gen 0 for a separate heap for large objects.

choices: Gen 0 of the small object heap
The current thread's stack
The large object heap
Unmanaged memory outside the GC heap
quiz.explanation: Any object of 85,000 bytes or more is allocated on the large object heap instead of in gen 0, and a byte array of 100,000 elements is about 100,000 bytes. The LOH is collected only together with gen 2 and is not compacted by default, which is why big temporary buffers are expensive. An array is a reference type, so it never lives on the thread's stack, and it is managed memory, not unmanaged.

quiz.prompt: Which of these allocates on the heap?
choices: `int x = 5;`
`object o = 5;`
`Span<int> s = stackalloc int[3];`
quiz.explanation: Assigning an int to an `object` variable boxes it: the runtime allocates a new box on the heap, copies the 5 into it and stores a reference to that box. `int x = 5` stays a plain value in the local, and `(1, 2)` is a ValueTuple, a struct, so it allocates nothing either. A common mistake is to count stackalloc as a heap allocation; it reserves memory in the current stack frame, which is released when the method returns.

choices: The span version parses without allocating a new string
They compile to the same code after JIT inlining
The span version copies the four chars to the stack
Substring shares memory with the original, so neither allocates
quiz.explanation: `AsSpan()[..4]` is a ReadOnlySpan<char> that points at the first four chars of the existing string, and int.Parse has an overload that reads a span directly, so no string is created. `Substring(0, 4)` copies those chars into a new string object on every call: a .NET string never shares memory with the string it came from. JIT inlining does not remove that allocation, and the span version copies nothing, to the stack or anywhere else.

quiz.prompt: `var arr = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }; var t = arr.AsSpan(1); t[0] = 9;` What is arr now?
choices: It throws
quiz.explanation: `AsSpan(1)` creates a view that starts at index 1 of the same array, so the span's index 0 is the array's index 1. Writing through the span stores the value straight into the array's memory, at the offset. A span never copies elements, so the array is not left unchanged, and an offset of 1 is within bounds, so nothing throws. Expecting the change at the array's index 0 forgets the offset.

quiz.prompt: Why can a `Span<T>` not be a field of a class or survive an `await`?
choices: It is too large to be copied into a heap object
It is a ref struct that must live on the stack
It is not thread-safe, so the compiler forbids sharing
It pins its array, and pins cannot outlive a method
quiz.explanation: `Span<T>` is declared as a `ref struct`, and the compiler keeps such a type on the stack: no class fields, no boxing, no lambda capture, and no local alive across an `await`, because an async method moves its locals into a heap state machine. The reason is safety: a span may point at `stackalloc` memory that dangles once the method returns. Size and thread safety have nothing to do with it, and an ordinary span pins nothing. Store a Memory<T> instead.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(10) is true?
choices: It returns an array of exactly 10, freshly zeroed
It returns an array of at least 10 that you must Return
It allocates the array on the stack, like stackalloc
It returns a pooled array that the GC returns for you
quiz.explanation: The shared pool keeps arrays in buckets sized in powers of two, so Rent(10) gives you an array of 16 elements: use only the length you asked for. It does not zero the array either, so a rented buffer can still hold bytes the last renter wrote. The GC knows nothing about the pool: an array you forget to hand back is just collected, and the pool allocates a new one later. Pooled arrays are ordinary heap arrays, not stack memory like stackalloc.

quiz.prompt: A lambda captures a local variable. What extra allocations can that cause?
choices: None: captured locals stay on the stack frame
A closure object for captured locals, plus a delegate
A new thread-local copy of each captured variable
A boxed copy of every local in the method, captured or not
quiz.explanation: The compiler moves captured locals into a generated closure class, so each capture costs that object plus the delegate that points at it. Only captured variables move; the other locals stay where they were, and no thread-local copies are made.

quiz.prompt: Your CRUD endpoint is slow. Where should you look first?
choices: String allocations that spans could replace
Database round-trips, missing indexes and N+1 queries
GC settings, such as server or workstation mode
Boxing in LINQ pipelines and captured lambdas
quiz.explanation: In a typical CRUD API the request spends most of its time waiting for the database. One round-trip costs milliseconds, while an allocation costs nanoseconds; an N+1 pattern multiplies the round-trips, and a missing index turns a lookup into a scan. Replacing strings with spans, removing boxing or switching between server and workstation GC trims microseconds, which is worth it only in a hot path that a profiler has pointed at.

quiz.prompt: Which tool reports allocated bytes per benchmark?
choices: BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser]
A Stopwatch wrapped around the benchmarked code
The debugger's locals window
dotnet test with code coverage on
quiz.explanation: BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser] reports allocated bytes and GC counts per operation, so you can measure an optimisation instead of guessing. A Stopwatch measures time only, and the debugger and code coverage say nothing about allocations.

flashcards.front: Value types on the stack: the precise version
flashcards.back: Value types live wherever their container lives: a local in the stack frame, a field inside its object on the heap.

flashcards.front: How does the generational GC work?
flashcards.back: New objects start in gen 0, which is collected often and cheaply; survivors move up to gen 1 and gen 2, collected less often.

flashcards.front: What is the large object heap?
flashcards.back: Where objects of 85,000 bytes or more are allocated; it is collected with gen 2, so churning big arrays is costly.
New strings from string operations, boxing, closures from capturing lambdas, LINQ iterators and delegates, and params arrays.
A view over contiguous memory (array, string or stack) that slices without copying.
Span is a stack-only ref struct for synchronous code; Memory can be stored in fields and used across await.
They may be larger than requested, must be returned to the pool, and must not be touched after being returned.
In measured hot paths such as parsing, serialisation and per-request middleware; elsewhere clarity wins.

drills.title: Parse an ISO date without allocating
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our log importer parses 50 million timestamps, and a profile shows most time in GC from Substring calls. Rewrite the date parser so it allocates nothing."

**Why it matters.** Slicing a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` and parsing the slices directly avoids creating three temporary strings per date. The validation rules stay exactly the same.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function `bool TryParseIsoDate(ReadOnlySpan<char> s, out int year, out int month, out int day)`:
- the text must be exactly 10 characters: four digits, `-`, two digits, `-`, two digits (ASCII digits only; no signs or spaces)
- the month must be 1 to 12 and the day must exist in that month and year (leap years included)
- on success return true with the parts; on failure return false (the out values are then 0)
- the method must not allocate on the managed heap (no Substring, Split, ToString or new strings)

**Worked example.** `"2024-02-29"` parses (2024 is a leap year); `"2023-02-29"` does not.
hints: A ReadOnlySpan can be indexed and sliced like a string, and int.Parse accepts a span slice directly.

Check the total length and where the separators sit, confirm every other position is a digit, convert the three slices without creating substrings, and finally ask the calendar whether that day exists in that month.

Confirm the overall shape and that the right positions hold digits before converting anything, read the year, month and day straight from slices of the input, and accept the date only if that month really has that day.

drills.title: Bug hunt: parse an ISO date without allocating
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "Parse an ISO date without allocating". It compiles and passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec of the local function `bool TryParseIsoDate(ReadOnlySpan<char> s, out int year, out int month, out int day)` is unchanged:
- the text must be exactly 10 characters: four digits, `-`, two digits, `-`, two digits (ASCII digits only; no signs or spaces)
- the month must be 1 to 12 and the day must exist in that month and year (leap years included)
- on success return true with the parts; on failure return false (the out values are then 0)
- the method must not allocate on the managed heap (no Substring, Split, ToString or new strings)
drills.explanation: The answers are right, but `s.ToString()` and every `Substring` create a new string on each call, four strings per parse. The test "parsing allocates nothing (boundary)" runs 1,000 parses and allows under 1,000 bytes; this version allocates about 144 KB, so it fails while every other test passes. `int.Parse` accepts a `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, so parse slices of the span directly: `int.Parse(s[..4])`, `int.Parse(s.Slice(5, 2))` and `int.Parse(s.Slice(8, 2))`. A slice is a view into the caller's memory, so it allocates nothing.
hints: Read the three lines that turn the year, month and day into numbers, and the line just before them.
A slice of a span points into the same memory, while a substring copies characters into a new object.
Parse the year, month and day from slices of the span instead of from substrings.
